name: Interview probability, set 1
description: Probability questions of the kind interviewers ask: dice games, coupons, patterns, hats, cards, urns, Bayes, ruin, ants and sticks. Each item keeps its own schedule.

items.prose: Roll a fair ten-sided die, faces 1 to 10, and be paid the face in pounds. After the first roll you may reroll once. If you do, you must keep the second roll.
items.question: What is the game worth with the best rule, in pounds?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare each first roll with the value of a fresh roll.

byKey.no-reroll: You never rerolled. A first roll of 1 to 5 is worth less than the 5.50 a fresh roll averages.
byKey.best-of-two: You kept the better of two rolls. Once you reroll, the first roll is gone, so the larger face is not yours.
byKey.keep-seven: You rerolled a 6 as well. A 6 beats the 5.50 a fresh roll is worth, so keep it.

explain.text: Reroll when the first roll is below 5.5, the value of a fresh roll. You keep 6 to 10 half the time, worth 8 on average. So the game is worth 0.5 × 8 + 0.5 × 5.5 = £6.75.

items.prose: Roll two fair twelve-sided dice, faces 1 to 12. You are paid the smaller face in pounds.
items.question: Which is the fair value, to the nearest penny?

options.why: You took the average of one die. The smaller of two faces sits below that average.
That is the expected larger face. The smaller face is 13 minus it on average.
You took 1 off the average of one die. Sum the chances that the smaller face is at least k instead.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the chance that both dice are at least k, then add over k.

explain.text: The smaller face is at least k when both dice are, with chance ((13 − k)/12)². Adding over k gives (1² + 2² + ⋯ + 12²)/144 = 650/144 ≈ £4.51. The larger face takes the rest of 13: 13 − 4.51 = £8.49.

items.prose: A fair four-sided die needs 25/3, about 8.33 rolls on average, to show every face. The interviewer then hands you a fair eight-sided die.
items.question: How many rolls do you expect until all eight faces have shown? Give two decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Split the wait into stages, one for each new face.

byKey.doubled: You doubled the four-sided answer. The last faces of eight are much harder to hit, so the wait more than doubles.
byKey.no-first: You left out the first roll, which always shows a new face. Add 1 for it.
byKey.squared: You used 8 × 8. Add a geometric wait for each new face instead: 8/8, 8/7, and so on.

explain.text: With k faces seen, a new face takes 8/(8 − k) rolls on average. Adding the eight stages gives 8(1 + 1/2 + ⋯ + 1/8) = 761/35 ≈ 21.74. Doubling the faces from four more than doubles the wait.

items.prose: A bag holds counters of five colours in equal numbers. You draw a counter, note its colour and put it back. You do this 8 times.
items.question: How many different colours do you expect to see? Give three decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Give each colour an indicator and add their chances.

byKey.missing: You found the expected number of colours never seen. Take it from 5.
byKey.one-colour: That is the chance one given colour appears. Add it over all five colours.

explain.text: Give each colour an indicator: 1 if it appears in the 8 draws. A colour is missed with chance (4/5)⁸ ≈ 0.1678, so it appears with chance 0.8322. Linearity adds the five: 5 × 0.8322 ≈ 4.161.

items.prose: A coin lands heads with chance 1/3 and tails with chance 2/3. You flip it until the pattern TTH first appears.
items.question: How many flips do you expect? Give two decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write an equation for each state: nothing, T, and TT.

byKey.fair: You used a fair coin. Here a tail comes up two times in three.
byKey.letters: You added the waits for each letter: 3/2 + 3/2 + 3. A head that comes too early sends you back, so set up the states.
byKey.swapped: You swapped the chances. Heads has chance 1/3, so TTH has chance (2/3)² × 1/3 = 4/27.

explain.text: From TT only an H finishes and a T keeps you at TT, so E_TT = 3. Then E_T = 3 + E_0/3 and E_0 = 1 + E_0/3 + (2/3)E_T. Solving gives E_0 = 27/4 = 6.75, which is 1/P(TTH) as TTH cannot overlap itself.

items.prose: Flip a fair coin until a given pattern of four flips appears. One player waits for HTHT, another for HHTT.
items.question: Whose wait is longer on average?

options.text: HTHT, 20 flips against 16: it overlaps itself at HT, so its copies bunch together.
Neither: each takes 16 flips, since any four flips show either pattern with chance 1/16.
options.why: You used 1/(1/16) for both. That holds only for a pattern that cannot overlap itself, like HHTT.

options.text: HHTT, 20 flips against 16: HH is the harder start.
options.why: You gave the overlap to the wrong pattern. No start of HHTT matches its end, so its wait is 16.

options.text: HTHT, 18 flips against 16: the overlap adds 2.
options.why: An overlap of two flips adds 2² = 4, not 2. So HTHT takes 16 + 4 = 20.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check where each pattern's start matches its own end.

explain.text: Add 2ᵏ for every k where the first k flips of the pattern equal its last k. HHTT matches only at k = 4, giving 16. HTHT matches at k = 2 and k = 4, giving 4 + 16 = 20.

items.prose: You flip a fair coin n times.
items.question: What is the smallest n that gives at least one head with chance above 99%?

widget.accept: 7: the chance of no head is 1/128, under 1%.
widget.label: Smallest n

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find when the chance of all tails drops below 1%.

byKey.six: Six flips miss every head with chance 1/64, about 1.6%. That is still above 1%.
byKey.hundred: You treated the chances as adding. The miss chance halves with each flip, so it falls below 1% fast.

explain.text: At least one head fails only when every flip is a tail, with chance (1/2)ⁿ. That is below 1% once 2ⁿ > 100. 2⁶ = 64 falls short and 2⁷ = 128 passes, so n = 7.

items.prose: Five people leave their coats at a cloakroom. The coats come back in a random order, one to each person.
items.question: What is the chance that exactly two people get their own coat? Give four decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Choose who matches, then count the ways the rest all miss.

byKey.no-derange: You chose the two who match but let the other three do anything. All three must miss: only 2 of their 6 orders do.
byKey.binomial: You treated the people as independent with chance 1/5 each. The coats are shared out, so the matches depend on each other.
byKey.poisson: You used the large-group limit 1/(2e). With five people, count exactly.

explain.text: Choose the two who match in C(5, 2) = 10 ways. The other three must all miss, and 2 of their 6 orders do. So the chance is 10 × 2/120 = 1/6 ≈ 0.1667.

items.prose: Two cards are dealt from a shuffled full deck. You are told only that the first card is red.
items.question: What is the chance the second card is a heart? Give four decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Split on the suit of the red first card.

byKey.was-heart: You assumed the first card was a heart. It is a diamond half the time, which leaves all 13 hearts.
byKey.was-diamond: You assumed the first card was a diamond. It is a heart half the time, which leaves 12 hearts.
byKey.ignored: You ignored the first card. Knowing it is red removes a heart half the time.

explain.text: The red first card is a heart or a diamond, each with chance 1/2. That leaves 12 or 13 hearts among 51 cards. So the chance is (12/51 + 13/51)/2 = 25/102 ≈ 0.2451.

items.prose: An urn holds 7 red and 3 blue balls. You draw without replacement until the first blue ball appears.
items.question: How many red balls do you expect to draw before it? Give two decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think of the blue balls as cutting the reds into equal gaps.

byKey.ratio: You divided the reds by the blues. Three blues cut the reds into four gaps, so divide by 4.
byKey.half: You took half the reds. Only the gap before the first blue counts, one of four.
byKey.share: You found the share of balls that are red. Count the reds in the first gap instead.

explain.text: The 3 blue balls cut the 7 reds into 4 gaps of equal expected size. The first gap holds 7/4 = 1.75 reds on average. Dividing by 3 forgets the gap after the last blue.

items.prose: A data check flags 90% of mispriced quotes and 3% of correct ones. One quote in 100 is mispriced.
items.question: A quote is flagged. What is the chance it is mispriced? Give four decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Picture 10,000 quotes and count the flags of each kind.

byKey.hit-rate: You gave the chance a mispriced quote is flagged. You need the reverse: the share of flags that are mispriced.
byKey.joint: You found the chance a quote is both mispriced and flagged. Divide by the chance a quote is flagged at all.
byKey.specificity: You gave the chance a correct quote passes. That says nothing yet about the flagged ones.

explain.text: Picture 10,000 quotes: 100 are mispriced and 90 of those are flagged. Of the 9,900 correct ones, 3% or 297 are flagged. So 90 of the 387 flagged quotes are mispriced: 0.2326.

items.prose: You hold £4 and bet £1 on each flip of a fair coin. You stop on reaching £10 or £0. You reach £10 with chance 4/10.
items.question: How many bets do you expect to make?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Set up first-step equations for the expected number of bets.

byKey.square: You squared the start, 4². The rule is k(N − k): the distance to each end, multiplied.
byKey.other-end: You squared the distance to £10. Multiply the two distances instead: 4 × 6.
byKey.product: You multiplied the start by the target. Use the distance to the top, 10 − 4, not 10.

explain.text: First-step analysis gives D_k = 1 + (D_{k−1} + D_{k+1})/2 with D_0 = D_10 = 0. Its solution is D_k = k(10 − k). From £4 that is 4 × 6 = 24 bets.

items.prose: Four independent numbers are drawn uniformly between 0 and 1.
items.question: What is the chance the largest exceeds 0.8?

options.why: That is the chance all four are below 0.8. The largest exceeds 0.8 in every other case.
You added 0.2 four times. The events overlap, so their chances do not add.
That is the chance all four exceed 0.8. Only the largest needs to.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the chance the largest is below 0.8 first.

explain.text: The largest is below 0.8 only when all four are: 0.8⁴ = 0.4096. So it exceeds 0.8 with chance 1 − 0.4096 = 0.5904.

items.prose: Twenty ants stand at random points of a 3 m rod, each facing left or right at random. All walk at 1 m a minute. Two ants that meet both turn round, and an ant that reaches an end falls off.
items.question: How many minutes do you expect until the last ant falls off? Give three decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Treat bouncing ants as ants that pass through each other.

byKey.worst: You gave the longest the last ant can take. On average the slowest of 20 ghosts finishes a little earlier.
byKey.one-ant: You gave one ant's average time. You need the last of 20, the largest of 20 such times.
byKey.unit-rod: You used a 1 m rod. Scale by 3 for the 3 m rod.

explain.text: Bouncing ants leave the same set of positions as ants that pass through, so each fall time is a ghost's. A ghost needs a uniform time between 0 and 3 minutes. The last of 20 such times averages 3 × 20/21 ≈ 2.857.

items.prose: Break a stick of length 1 at two independent uniform points, making three pieces.
items.question: What is the chance the longest piece is longer than 0.4? Give two decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use inclusion and exclusion over the three pieces.

byKey.no-overlap: You added 0.36 for each piece. Below a half two pieces can both be long, so take off the overlaps.
byKey.complement: That is the chance every piece is at most 0.4. Take it from 1.
byKey.half-rule: You used the answer for a half. With 0.4 the long pieces can overlap, which changes the count.

explain.text: A given piece exceeds 0.4 with chance 0.6² = 0.36, and two given pieces both do with chance 0.2² = 0.04. Inclusion and exclusion gives 3 × 0.36 − 3 × 0.04 = 0.96. Three pieces cannot all exceed 0.4.
